paras: The seizure of Tom Bibb was the capture of a Black man near Fort Deposit, Madison County, Alabama, on about August 13, 1900, by a mob of Lincoln County, Tennessee, citizens who accused him of assaulting Mrs. Alonzo Gillham and carried him across the state line. Jailed under his captors' promise that he would be hanged if proven guilty, he was saved by an alibi from State Senator Ed L. Pulley and returned to Huntsville two weeks later.

On the afternoon of August 9, according to a Huntsville special, a Black man came to the door of Mrs. Gillham's home near Lincoln post office and assaulted her before fleeing; she was found unconscious. A mob that included men from Fayetteville, Tennessee, followed the trail into Madison County, Alabama, and sent for bloodhounds. The next day the mob seized Jim Scott, described as "colored," north of Gurley, but he "proved to be the wrong man and was turned loose." A Chattanooga deputy sheriff's bloodhounds could not follow the cold scent, and private citizens offered a reward.

On August 13 a "determined band of men" captured a Black man near Fort Deposit who was said to match Mrs. Gillham's description. That night the mob carried him from Huntsville into Lincoln County, to Lincoln in the Age-Herald's account and to Fayetteville in the Courier-Journal's. On August 14 he was brought before Mrs. Gillham, who identified him, while he insisted that he had been working that day for Senator Pulley at his summer home on Monte Sano.

The mob agreed to wait for Pulley, who identified the man as his worker and wrote to Mrs. Gillham that he had been at Monte Sano that day. Mrs. Gillham then sent the mob a letter, read aloud by her father, expressing "some doubt" that he was the right man, and her husband urged the mob to be careful. The mob named a committee to investigate the alibi and placed him in the Lincoln County jail on the understanding that he would be "turned over to the people to be hanged if proven guilty."

On August 16, amid fear of mob violence at Fayetteville, Bibb was moved to the jail in Nashville. A Huntsville dispatch said Sheriff H. R. Melson made the move despite promising the mob not to, a promise the Camden Chronicle called illegal. The committee continued to gather evidence in Madison County and by August 17 further mob action seemed "hardly probable."

On August 21 a Nashville special reported "every probability" that Bibb was innocent, because the committee's evidence supported his account. According to a Huntsville special of August 27, Pulley proved the alibi, the mob leaders came to believe him innocent, and Bibb returned to Huntsville on August 26.

The first reports, in the Age-Herald, the Courier-Journal and wire copy in Indianapolis, St. Paul and St. Louis, treated the assault as established, under headlines such as "BIG MOB AFTER ANOTHER NEGRO" and "HUNTING DOWN A FIEND." Once Bibb was captured, the Age-Herald described his captors as "the best citizens of Lincoln County" unwilling to punish the innocent, while headlining "SENATOR PULLEY SAVES A NEGRO FROM BEING LYNCHED." The Courier-Journal's headline put the case as a "QUESTION OF IDENTITY" that alone was saving him "From the Fury of a Tennessee Mob."

The Camden Chronicle printed the mob's insistence that it had "the right negro" and would "get their man" under the headline "MOB DISAPPOINTED." The Cleveland Gazette, the only Black paper found to cover the case, wrote on September 8 that the mob, "in sheer pretense of sincerity," held the man after the alibi was verified and still sought "their victim." It doubted Mrs. Gillham's charge, suggesting "over-readiness" to "wreak vengeance upon a poor and unfortunate race."

Accounts differ on the committee's finding: the Camden Chronicle dispatch said it had proof of guilt, while the later Nashville and Huntsville specials, borne out by his release, said the evidence supported the alibi. The Age-Herald said Mrs. Gillham "positively identified" him before writing of her doubts, whereas the Gazette said she acknowledged a "probable mistake" and with her husband asked his release. His name appears as Tom Bibb, Bibbs and Gibbs.

reader.title: Seizure of Tom Bibb by a Lincoln County, Tennessee, mob
bases: A mob from Lincoln County, Tennessee, seized a Black man in Madison County, Alabama, carried him across the state line and held him on a promise that he would be hanged if found guilty; no killing occurred (A8, A10, A11, A17).

A mob of Lincoln County citizens seized Bibb over an alleged assault and threatened to hang him if found guilty, but he was jailed, moved to Nashville and returned alive to Huntsville (A11, A13, A17); with no one killed, this was a threatened lynching, not a lynching.

Separate Huntsville, Fayetteville and Nashville specials in the Age-Herald and Courier-Journal, a Huntsville dispatch in the Camden Chronicle and a Cleveland Gazette editorial agree on the capture, the alibi and the jailing (A8, A11, A13, A16, A18), though they disagree on whether the committee found him guilty.

accounts.label: Huntsville and Fayetteville specials (Age-Herald, Courier-Journal)
accounts.gist: A mob of Lincoln County citizens captured Bibb, carried him to Tennessee, where Mrs. Gillham identified him; Senator Pulley's alibi and her letter of doubt led the mob to jail him pending a committee's inquiry.

accounts.label: Mob's claim (Camden Chronicle dispatch)
accounts.gist: The committee said it had proof Bibbs was 'the right negro', that the alibi had failed, and that the mob would 'get their man' despite his removal to Nashville.

accounts.label: Nashville and Huntsville follow-ups
accounts.gist: The committee's evidence supported Bibb's alibi; Pulley proved it, and Bibb returned to Huntsville.

accounts.label: Black editorial (Cleveland Gazette)
accounts.gist: After the alibi was verified Mrs. Gillham admitted a 'probable mistake' and with her husband asked his release, but the mob held him and kept seeking a victim.

framing.detail: The first Age-Herald and wire reports treated the assault as fact ('BIG MOB AFTER ANOTHER NEGRO', 'HUNTING DOWN A FIEND') and reported the manhunt without criticism.
Later reports praised the mob as 'the best citizens' unwilling to punish the innocent while headlining 'SENATOR PULLEY SAVES A NEGRO FROM BEING LYNCHED'.
The Camden Chronicle relayed the mob's resolve to 'get their man' while noting the sheriff's promise to the mob was illegal.
The Cleveland Gazette called the mob 'bad men' in 'lawless defiance' and doubted the woman's charge.

info: Manhunt from Aug. 9; capture near Fort Deposit reported Aug. 13; carried to Tennessee night of Aug. 13; identification and alibi Aug. 14; removed to Nashville Aug. 16; back in Huntsville Aug. 26.

Captured near Fort Deposit (Huntsville dispatch); carried from Huntsville to Lincoln, Tenn. (Age-Herald) or Fayetteville, Tenn. (Courier-Journal); held in Lincoln County jail at Fayetteville, then Nashville jail.
Tom Bibb (also 'Bibbs', 'Tom Bibbs', 'Gibbs'), described as a 'negro' / 'colored man'; earlier, Jim Scott, 'colored', was seized north of Gurley and released as the wrong man.
A Black man was accused of assaulting Mrs. Alonzo Gillham at her home near Lincoln post office, Lincoln County, Tenn., on the afternoon of Aug. 9; she was found unconscious.
A mob of Lincoln County, Tenn., citizens, including men from Fayetteville, Tenn., described by the Age-Herald as 'the best citizens of Lincoln County'.
Bibb returned to Huntsville on Aug. 26 after Senator Pulley proved his alibi, per a Huntsville special; a Camden Chronicle dispatch earlier said the committee had found him the 'right negro'.
